UQ Gatton trials cancer drug that could cure dogs with terminal tumours
Date: Mon Feb  9 01:00:00 2026 UTC

UQ Gatton Professor Rachel Allavena said the drug Enzistat developed by American pharmaceutical company Avammune has the potential to treat cancers in dogs and humans. "It gives dogs in southeast Queensland another option, and it's always nice to do cutting edge trials," she said. "The early data that the company has is that it's helped dogs survive longer and have less bad side effects from their cancer. "We're quite hopeful that for dogs that might not have a lot of options that it might be a useful drug in the future." UQ is looking for 30 dogs with inoperable tumours and 30 dogs in palliative care to be part of the trial. Professor Allavena said they hope the drug can shrink inoperable tumours so they could be removed surgically and give a final hope for dogs in palliative care. "They don't have hope for a cure any other way, but their owners just want to see if they can keep them to be around a little longer and see if it can make them more comfortable," she said. She said a third to a half of dogs will get cancer and it is more common than in lots of other species. Professor Allavena has been researching immune-based cancer therapies for about 15 years and she said it was really hard at times. "It's really hard when we hear about one of our patients passing away," she said. "We do also get a lot of joy from giving people hope or giving the animals options." Anyone interested in joining the trial need a cancer diagnosis and referral from their vet. People involved in the trial would need to give a tablet to their dog twice a day for six weeks and need to come to UQ Gatton three times throughout the trial. The medication and any additional blood tests, biopsies, or examinations are provided as part of the study and owners have to cover any other veterinary costs. Contact uqvets.sa@uq.edu.au to join the trial.

Cats give genetic clues to better cancer treatments (https://www.ft.com/content/807ac68a-d96a-4da0-bdfc-5970c3c5a836)
【turn1041news19】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; A groundbreaking study led by the Wellcome Sanger Institute has revealed that domestic cats share significant genetic similarities with humans in the development of cancer, offering new avenues for treatment in both species. Researchers analyzed 13 types of feline tumors from nearly 500 cats across five countries by sequencing DNA from cancerous and healthy tissues. They found mutations in about 1,000 genes linked to human cancers, across various tumor types like blood, bone, lung, skin, gastrointestinal, and central nervous system cancers.

One key finding relates to feline breast cancer, where over half showed mutations in the FBXW7 gene—rare in humans but linked to worse outcomes. Tests with common chemotherapy drugs such as vincristine and vinorelbine successfully suppressed tumor growth in cat tissues with FBXW7 mutations. This discovery positions felines as potential early test subjects for treatments, especially where human clinical trials are harder to implement.

The research highlights the value of "comparative oncology," studying cancer across species, akin to research on elephants' resistance to tumors. Experts suggest these cross-species studies could offer vital insights into cancer prevention and treatment for humans.
Cats give genetic clues to better cancer treatments 
Date: Thu Feb 19 19:00:08 2026 UTC

Domestic cats have emerged as unlikely allies in the fight against human cancers, after scientists found close similarities between genetic changes that drive the deadly disease in both species.
The discoveries from the first large-scale DNA study of feline tumours open up new ideas for treatments for people and pets, researchers from the UK's Wellcome Sanger Institute said.  
Scientists are increasingly focusing on genetic lessons from animals that are prone to cancers or unusually resilient to them. Household species are of particular interest because they are exposed to some of the same environmental risks as their human companions.  
"By comparing cancer genomics across different species, we gain a greater understanding of what causes the disease," said Bailey Francis, a Wellcome Sanger researcher and co-first author of a paper published in the journal Science on Thursday. "This could help experts in the veterinary field as well as those studying cancer in humans."
The Wellcome Sanger researchers and colleagues from countries including Canada and Switzerland examined 13 cat cancer types using tissue samples collected by vets from almost 500 domestic animals across five countries. They sequenced DNA from tumours and healthy tissues to look for about 1,000 genes that are associated with cancer in people. The felines showed similar genetic mutations to humans in cases of blood, bone, lung, skin, gastrointestinal and central nervous system tumours.
One of the most intriguing findings was for cat breast cancers, more than half of which showed a mutation in a gene called FBXW7. The change is far rarer in human mammary cancers, but the prognosis for the sufferer is worse when it is present.
The researchers found that the chemotherapeutic drugs vincristine and vinorelbine, used to treat diseases such as leukaemia, curbed the growth of the FBXW7-mutated tumours in cat tissues. 
This suggested an initial test of the drugs' effectiveness against breast cancer could be done in felines, as a trial in people would be hard to organise because of the FBXW7 mutation's relative scarcity.

Cats could help scientists better understand human cancer, study says (https://www.washingtonpost.com/lifestyle/2026/05/30/scientists-find-cancer-gene-similarities-cats-humans-study-says/)
【turn1041news20】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 4 months ago; A recent study led by Louise van der Weyden and international researchers has discovered significant genetic similarities between feline and human cancers, offering promising avenues for shared treatment advancements. Analyzing tumor samples from nearly 500 domestic cats across multiple countries, the researchers identified common mutations in about 1,000 cat genes that correspond to human cancer genes. Among the most striking parallels was the FBXW7 gene, a tumor suppressor found mutated in both feline mammary tumors and human breast cancer, associated with poor prognoses.

Published in the journal Science, the research underlines cats as effective disease models due to their genetic closeness to humans and shared living environments that expose them to similar carcinogens. The study also revealed chemotherapy drug vincristine’s effectiveness in treating feline mammary tumors, providing a potential pathway for clinical trials and the development of targeted treatments. While experts like Jaime Modiano stress that more research is needed, the findings mark a significant step toward dual-species cancer therapy, benefiting both feline and human patients.
Cats could help scientists better understand human cancer, study says
Date: Sat May 30 09:00:00 2026 UTC

Louise van der Weyden is a dog person. But as a scientist who studies cancer in animals, she has turned her attention to cats in recent years.
Insight into feline cancers has been like "a black box," van der Weyden said, because scientists have known so little about them.
But what she recently found after years of research surprised her: Cat cancers are similar to some human cancers, giving her hope for future advancement in treatments.
"It's a unique opportunity to help two species in one go," van der Weyden said.
The finding came from a study in which van der Weyden and other scientists across the world investigated cancer-causing genes in tumor samples of nearly 500 domestic cats - specifically which genes were commonly mutated.
The most striking similarity was in a gene called FBXW7, a critical tumor suppressor for people and cats. In cats, the gene was frequently altered in mammary tumors. Mutations in the gene are also associated with worse outcomes for people who have breast cancer.
Cancer progresses faster in dogs than in people, meaning researchers can receive quicker results with potential treatments in clinical trials with canines. The bone cancer osteosarcoma is more common in dogs than people, so scientists have learned techniques from the animals on how to treat people with the same cancer, and vice versa.
A decade ago, researchers told The Washington Post that dogs were observed more than cats in oncology studies because less was known about feline tumors and cats tended to become more stressed interacting with people.
For their study, van der Weyden and other researchers collected tissue samples from domestic cats from Austria, Canada, England, Germany, New Zealand and Scotland. 
They screened about 1,000 cat genes that are equivalent to human genes associated with cancer. Van der Weyden said she worried they might not find similarities between cat and human cancers, partly because few cat genetic studies had been completed. 
However, in addition to the gene associated with breast cancer in both species, researchers said they found similarities in human and cat cancers affecting their blood, bones, lungs, skin, gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system.
"I was first of all doing it for the cat," said van der Weyden, senior staff scientist at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, a genomics research center in Cambridgeshire, England. "But then to find that there are similarities and we can help humans, that's fantastic."
Researchers found that the chemotherapy drug vincristine was effective against cats' mammary tumors, according to the study, which was published in February. They said that finding could guide veterinary pharmaceutical companies in developing treatment for mammary cancer, which is the third-most-common feline cancer and is typically deadly, according to Cornell University's Feline Health Center.
"Before we just didn't know; we didn't know what drug you could potentially pick," said Wood, who teaches pathology at the University of Guelph in Ontario. "And now there's sort of a list, at least, that could then proceed to clinical trials."
Jaime Modiano, a professor at the University of Minnesota's school of veterinary medicine who was not involved in the research, said the study is a foundation for scientists to learn more about cat and human cancers. However, he said, much more research is required to determine whether the findings can lead to treatments for cats - let alone helping with human cancers.
"It's the first step," Modiano said, "in the journey of a thousand miles."

How cats may prove an unexpected ally in fight against cancer (https://www.thetimes.com/uk/science/article/cats-cancer-research-news-bgccsjdc5)
【turn1041news21】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 8 months ago; A groundbreaking study published in *Science* reveals that domestic cats may become key allies in the fight against cancer. Researchers from the Wellcome Sanger Institute, Ontario Veterinary College, and University of Bern analyzed tumors from 493 pet cats across five countries, covering 13 cancer types. Their findings show many feline cancers share the same genetic mutations as human cancers, making cats valuable models for understanding rare and aggressive human diseases, such as certain breast and bone cancers.

Of particular interest is feline mammary carcinoma, which mirrors aggressive and hard-to-treat forms of human breast cancer. The study identified seven key "driver" genes in these tumors, notably FBXW7, also associated with poor outcomes in humans. The most commonly damaged gene across all feline cancers was TP53, already known as the most frequently altered gene in human cancers.

The research is part of the "One Medicine" initiative, aiming to bridge veterinary and human medicine. Unlike lab mice, cats develop cancer naturally and share human environments, offering insight into environmental cancer risks. This genetic overlap and shared exposure may lead to better understanding, treatment, and possibly prevention strategies for cancer in both species.
How cats may prove an unexpected ally in fight against cancer
Date: Thu Feb 19 18:59:53 2026 UTC

A scientific study of hundreds of pet cats suggests that an unexpected ally in the fight against cancer may be curled up on the sofa.
Some cancers are frustratingly hard to study in people because they are rare. In cats, however, comparable tumours can be far more common. 
The research shows that many of these feline cancers are driven by the same genetic mutations as their human counterparts.
According to the scientists, studying the common animal versions of rare human diseases may reveal patterns and insights that would otherwise remain hidden.
One of the most promising areas is in the treatment of mammary tumours, which in cats are often incredibly aggressive and mirror some of the toughest-to-treat forms of human breast cancer.
The researchers found that many feline mammary tumours carry the same "faulty" genetic switches seen in women. That raises the possibility that drugs already used or being tested for human patients could be repurposed for cats. In turn, careful observation of how cats respond to them might help refine treatment strategies in people.
• Rhys Blakely: Monkeys or microchips? The debate over animal testing won't die
The study, published in the journal Science, is part of a broader approach known as "One Medicine", which is based on the idea that veterinary and human medicine should inform one another.
An international team led by the Wellcome Sanger Institute in Britain, the Ontario Veterinary College and the University of Bern analysed tumours from 493 pet cats across five countries, spanning 13 cancer types.
They examined the feline versions of roughly 1,000 genes known to be involved in human cancers, comparing DNA from each tumour with healthy tissue from the same animal. The result is the first comprehensive genetic map - or "oncogenome" - of cancer in domestic cats.
"The genetics of domestic cat tumours are no longer a 'black box'," said Louise van der Weyden of the Wellcome Sanger Institute, co-senior author of the study.

Rescue dog Rosie's cancer shrinks after world-first mRNA vaccine (https://www.theaustralian.com.au/business/technology/tech-boss-uses-ai-and-chatgpt-to-create-cancer-vaccine-for-his-dying-dog/news-story/292a21bcbe93efa17810bfcfcdfadbf7)
【turn1041news22】 [wordlim: 100] Published: 7 months ago; In a groundbreaking medical development, Sydney tech entrepreneur Paul Conyngham used artificial intelligence and mRNA technology to create a customized cancer vaccine for his rescue dog, Rosie. Diagnosed in 2024 with an aggressive mast cell tumor, traditional chemotherapy and surgery failed to stop the cancer. Determined to save her, Conyngham used ChatGPT and AI data processing to analyze Rosie's genomic data, identify cancer mutations, and design a personalized mRNA vaccine with help from experts at the University of NSW.

Developed in collaboration with the UNSW RNA Institute and administered by veterinary researchers at the University of Queensland, the vaccine significantly shrank one of Rosie's large tumors. This marks the first known case of a personalized mRNA cancer vaccine being developed for a dog.
